In February 2025, numerous planned protests occurred outside of Tesla showrooms and service centers throughout the US. The protests were in response to Musk's contentious actions as leader of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) at the beginning of Donald Trump's second term as US president.[439][440]

Lawsuits against Tesla critics and vehicle malfunction complainants in China

[edit]

On February 12, 2025, the Associated Press reported that in China, Tesla had sued six car owners, six or more bloggers, and two media outlets for defamation since 2021. The car owners had complained publicly about Tesla's quality and accidents caused by major mechanical malfunctions, like brake failure. The bloggers and media outlets had written critically about the company. As of the date of publication, the Associated Press reported that Tesla had won 11 verdicts, two judgments were on appeal, and one had been settled outside court.[441]

Criticism

[edit]
Main article: Criticism of Tesla, Inc.

Data privacy

[edit]

A Tesla vehicle was only the second product ever reviewed by the Mozilla Foundation that failed all of their privacy criteria.[442][443]

A Tesla owner filed a lawsuit in 2023 following a Reuters report that Tesla employees shared "highly invasive videos and images recorded by customers' car cameras" with one another.[444]

Internal data troves shared with various international government agencies and news organizations by former employee and whistleblower Lukasz Krupski in late 2023 implicated Tesla in "serious data protection lapse[s]."[445] The data Krupski retrieved included "information about current and former Tesla staff, including passport numbers, medical details and salaries" and was readily available on internal systems that most employees had access to.[446] As of November 2023, the Data Protection Authority in the Netherlands was investigating whether Tesla's alleged lack of internal security violated privacy laws.[447]

Short sellers

[edit]

TSLAQ is a collective of Tesla skeptics and short-sellers who are vocally critical of Tesla and aim to "shape [the] perception [of Tesla] and move its stock."[448] In January 2020, 20% of Tesla stock was shorted, the highest at that time of any stock in the US equity markets.[449] By early 2021, according to CNN, short sellers had lost $40 billion during 2020 as the stock price climbed much higher.[450] Michael Burry, a short seller portrayed in The Big Short, had shorted Tesla previously via his firm Scion Asset Management, but removed his position in October 2021.[451]

Tesla's mission

[edit]

According to automotive journalist Jamie Kitman, when multiple CEOs of major automotive manufacturers approached Tesla for EV technology that Musk had claimed the company was willing to share, they instead were offered the opportunity to buy regulatory credits from the company. This suggested, according to Kitman, that "the company may not be as eager for the electric revolution to occur as it claims."[452]

Giga New York audit

[edit]

In 2020, the New York State Comptroller released an audit of the Giga New York factory project, concluding that it presented many red flags, including a lack of basic due diligence and that the factory itself produced only $0.54 in economic benefits for every $1 spent by the state.[453][454][455]

Delays

[edit]

Musk has been criticized for repeatedly pushing out both production and release dates of products.[456][457] By one count in 2016, Musk had missed 20 projections.[458] In October 2017, Musk predicted that Model 3 production would be 5,000 units per week by December.[459] A month later, he revised that target to "sometime in March" 2018.[460] Delivery dates for the Model 3 were delayed as well.[461] Other projects like converting supercharger stations to be solar-powered have also lagged projections.[462] Musk responded in late 2018: "punctuality is not my strong suit...I never made a mass-produced car. How am I supposed to know with precision when it's gonna get done?"[463]

Accolades

[edit]

In 2019, Model 3 earned the Top Safety Pick+ Award from the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety.[464] In 2022, Model Y has received the highest safety score of any car analyzed under Euro NCAP.[465]

In 2022, Tesla won S&P Global Automotive Loyalty Awards in 7 categories.[466]

In 2025, TIME magazine named Model S as one of the best inventions of the past 25 years, praising it as a "game-changing advance for electric vehicles".[467]

Motor Trend has shortlisted Cybertruck for the magazine's 2025 Truck of the Year, praising its steer-by-wire system and other tech, but criticizing "the design's many compromises".[468]

Vehicle product issues

[edit]

Recalls

[edit]

On April 20, 2017, Tesla issued a worldwide recall of 53,000 (~70%) of the 76,000 vehicles it sold in 2016 due to faulty parking brakes which could become stuck and "prevent the vehicles from moving".[469][470] On March 29, 2018, Tesla issued a worldwide recall of 123,000 Model S cars built before April 2016 due to corrosion-susceptible power steering bolts, which could fail and require the driver to use "increased force" to control the vehicle.[471]

In October 2020, Tesla initiated a recall of nearly 50,000 Model X and Y vehicles throughout China for suspension issues.[472] Soon after in November, the NHTSA announced it had opened its investigation into 115,000 Tesla cars regarding "front suspension safety issues", citing specifically 2015–2017 Model S and 2016–2017 Model X years. Cases of the "whompy wheel" phenomenon, which also included Model X and the occasional Model 3 cars, have been documented through 2020.[473][474]

In February 2021, Tesla was required by the NHTSA to recall 135,000 Model S and Model X vehicles built from 2012 to 2018 due to using a flash memory device that was rated to last only 5 to 6 years.[475] The problem was related to touchscreen failures that could possibly affect the rearview camera, safety systems, Autopilot and other features.[476][477] The underlying technical reason is that the car writes a large amount of syslog content to the device, wearing it out prematurely.[478]

Also in February 2021, the German Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA) ordered Tesla to recall 12,300 Model X cars because of "body mouldings problems".[479][480]

In June 2021, Tesla recalled 5,974 electric vehicles due to worries that brake caliper bolts might become loose, which could lead to loss of tire pressure, increasing the chance of a crash.[481]

On December 30, 2021, Tesla announced that they are recalling more than 475,000 US model vehicles. This included 356,309 Model 3 Tesla vehicles from 2017 to 2020 due to rear-view camera issues and a further 119,009 Tesla Model S vehicles due to potential problems with the trunk or boot. The Model S recall includes vehicles manufactured between 2014 and 2021. Around 1% of recalled Model 3s may have a defective rear-view camera, and around 14% of recalled Model S may have the defect. The recall was not linked to a contemporaneous issue regarding the "Passenger Play" feature, which allowed games to be played on the touchscreen while the car is in motion.[482] After an investigation was launched by the NHTSA covering 585,000 vehicles, Tesla agreed to make changes where the feature would be locked and unusable while the car is moving.[483]

In September 2022, Tesla announced that they are recalling almost 1.1 million US model vehicles because the automatic window reversal system might not react correctly after detecting an obstruction, increasing the risk of injury.[484][485] In response,[clarification needed] Tesla announced an over-the-air software fix.[485]

In February 2023, Tesla recalled its FSD software following a recommendation from NHTSA; the recall applied to approximately 360,000 cars.[486] NHTSA found that FSD caused "unreasonable risk" when used on city streets.[487] In March 2023, about 3,500 Model Y Teslas were recalled for a bolting issue concerning the cars' second-row seats.[488]

In December 2023, following a 2-year investigation by the NHTSA,[489] Tesla issued a wider recall on all vehicles equipped with any version of Autosteer, including 2012–2023 Model S; 2016–2023 Model X; 2017–2023 Model 3; and 2020–2023 Model Y, covering 2,031,220 vehicles in total.[490] The NHTSA concluded that Autosteer's controls were not sufficient to prevent misuse and did not ensure that the drivers maintained "continuous and sustained responsibility for vehicle operation" and states that affected vehicles will receive an over-the-air software remedy.[490][491]

Fires

[edit]
See also: Plug-in electric vehicle fire incidents § Tesla

Tesla customers have reported the company as being "slow" to address how their cars can ignite.[492] In 2013, a Model S caught fire after the vehicle hit metal debris on a highway in Kent, Washington. Tesla confirmed the fire began in the battery pack and was caused by the impact of an object.[493] As a result of this and other incidents, Tesla announced its decision to extend its current vehicle warranty to cover fire damage.[494] In March 2014, the NHTSA announced that it had closed the investigation into whether the Model S was prone to catch fire, after Tesla said it would provide more protection to its battery packs.[495] All Model S cars manufactured after March 6, 2014, have had the 0.25-inch (6.4 mm) aluminum shield over the battery pack replaced with a new three-layer shield.[496] In October 2019, the NHTSA opened an investigation into possible battery defects in Tesla's Model S and X vehicles from 2012 to 2019 that could cause "non-crash" fires.[497][498][499]

Autopilot crashes

[edit]
See also: List of Tesla Autopilot crashes

A Model S driver died in a collision with a tractor-trailer in 2016, while the vehicle was in Autopilot mode; the driver is believed to be the first person to have died in a Tesla vehicle in Autopilot.[500][501] The NHTSA investigated the accident but found no safety-related defect trend.[502] In March 2018, a driver of a Tesla Model X was killed in a crash. Investigators say that the driver of the vehicle had his car in 'self-driving' mode and was using his phone to play games when the vehicle collided with the barrier in the middle of the freeway. Through investigation, the NTSB found that the Tesla malfunctioned due to the system being confused by an exit on the freeway.[503]

According to a document released in June 2021, the NHTSA has initiated at least 30 investigations into Tesla crashes that were believed to involve the use of Autopilot, with some involving fatalities.[504][505] In early September 2021, the NHTSA updated the list with an additional fatality incident[506] and ordered Tesla to hand over all extensive[clarification needed] data pertaining to US cars with Autopilot to determine if there is a safety defect that leads Tesla cars to collide with first-responder vehicles.[506][507][508] In late September 2021, Tesla released an over-the-air software update to detect emergency lights at night.[509] In October 2021, the NHTSA asked Tesla why it did not issue a recall when it sent out that update.[510] In June 2022, the NHTSA said it would expand its probe, extending it to 830,000 cars from all current Tesla models. The probe was moved up from the Preliminary Evaluation level to Engineering Analysis. The regulator cited the reason for the expansion as the need to "explore the degree to which Autopilot and associated Tesla systems may exacerbate human factors or behavioral safety risks by undermining the effectiveness of the driver's supervision."[511]

A safety test conducted by the Dawn Project in August 2022 demonstrated that a test driver using the beta version of Full Self-Driving repeatedly hit a child-sized mannequin in its path,[512] but there has been controversy over its conclusions.[513] Several Tesla owners responded by conducting their own, independent tests using children; NHTSA released a statement warning against the practice.[514]

In 2025, the California DMV filed a lawsuit against Tesla, claiming it had misled drivers about its vehicles' self-driving capabilities. The DMV sought to suspend Tesla's sales and manufacturing in the state of California for a minimum of 30 days.[515][516]

Software hacking

[edit]

In August 2015, two researchers said they were able to take control of a Tesla Model S by hacking into the car's entertainment system.[517] The hack required the researchers to physically access the car.[518] Tesla issued a security update for the Model S the day after the exploit was announced.[519]

In September 2016, researchers at Tencent's Keen Security Lab demonstrated a remote attack on a Tesla Model S and controlled the vehicle in both Parking and Driving Mode without physical access. They were able to compromise the automotive networking bus (CAN bus) when the vehicle's web browser was used while the vehicle was connected to a malicious Wi-Fi hotspot.[520] This was the first case of a remote control exploit demonstrated on a Tesla. The vulnerability was disclosed to Tesla under their bug bounty program and patched within 10 days, before the exploit was made public.[521] Tencent also hacked the doors of a Model X in 2017.[522]

In January 2018, security researchers informed Tesla that an Amazon Web Services account of theirs could be accessed directly from the Internet and that the account had been exploited for cryptocurrency mining. Tesla responded by securing the compromised system, rewarding the security researchers financially via their bug bounty program, and stating that the compromise did not violate customer privacy, nor vehicle safety or security.[523][524] Later in 2019, Tesla awarded a car and $375,000 to ethical hackers during a Pwn2Own Model 3 hacking event.[525]

In June 2022, Martin Herfurt, a security researcher in Austria, discovered that changes made to make Tesla vehicles easier to start with NFC cards also allowed for pairing new keys to the vehicle, allowing an attacker to enroll their keys to a vehicle.[526]

Phantom braking

[edit]

In February 2022, Tesla drivers reported a surge in "phantom braking" events when using Tesla Autopilot, which coincides with the automaker's removal of radar as a supplemental sensor in May 2021.[527] In response, NHTSA opened an investigation the same month.[528] In August 2022, a consumer class action was filed alleging that the Autopilot system in Tesla cars "contains a hazardous defect which causes the vehicle to suddenly and unintentionally brake".[529][530] In November 2024, Tesla failed to persuade a US District Judge to dismiss the lawsuit.[531] The next court date is January 7, 2025.[531]

In May 2023, German business newspaper Handelsblatt published a series of articles based on a trove of internal Tesla data submitted to them from informants.[532] The 100 gigabytes of data "contain[ed] over 1,000 accident reports involving phantom braking or unintended acceleration" as well as complaints about Tesla Autopilot.[533] Dutch authorities responded by saying they were investigating the company for possible data privacy violations.[534]

In February 2025, a German court declared Tesla Autopilot defective for normal use due to phantom braking issues.[535]

In February 2025, a group of Australian buyers sued Tesla with a class action over multiple issues like battery range, driving assistance, and phantom braking.[536]

Driving range performance

[edit]

Tesla has received thousands of complaints from owners that the driving ranges of their vehicles did not meet the ranges advertised by Tesla or the projections of in-dash range meters. When service centers were overwhelmed with appointments to take care of these issues, Tesla established a diversion team to cancel as many appointments as possible. Customers were told that remote diagnostics had determined there was no problem, and their appointments were canceled. The company has been fined by South Korean regulators for its exaggerated range estimates.[537]

Vehicle sales

[edit]

In 2024, Tesla ranked as the world's best-selling battery electric passenger car manufacturer, with a market share of 17.6%.[538] Tesla reported 2023 vehicle deliveries of 1.8 million units, up 38% from 2022.[539][540] In March 2024, Tesla produced its six millionth car.[541] In Q4 2023, BYD took over the top spot for EVs shipped, but Tesla regained the title in Q1 2024.[542]

Tesla sells the most vehicles in the US (674,000+ in 2023) and has received $11.4 billion in regulatory credits from federal and state governments. The federal government previously provided a $7500 rebate to customers.[543][544][545] Tesla received around $426 million from the Chinese government for cars manufactured at its Shanghai facility.[546] Germany was Tesla's third-largest market in 2023, selling 63,682 units. Germany ended its EV subsidy program in December 2023. Under the program, a €6,750 discount was provided with Tesla paying €2,250. Tesla announced it would cover the entire discount going forward.[547] In 2023, over 63,000 Teslas were sold in France with customers receiving up to €7,000 via the bonus écologique. The government decreased the budget for EV aid from €1.5 billion to €700 million in 2024.[548] Canada was in Tesla's top five markets in 2023 with over 52,000 vehicles sold. In 2025, Tesla was accused of having "a run on the bank" when it sold a historic 8,600 vehicles in 72 hours before Canada's EV rebate program's funds were depleted. Tesla claimed 4000 vehicles alone were sold over one weekend in Quebec City.[549][550] The Government of Canada announced on March 25, 2025, that it had suspended the rebates and was investigating. The government also declared Tesla would be ineligible for any future rebates as long as the US tariffs on Canadian products continued.[551] Musk has stated he is against government subsidies but will take them if they are available.[552]

Sales have been negatively impacted by Musk's actions during the second Trump presidency.[553][554] Tesla sales have decreased worldwide (the most in countries like France, Germany, the UK, Sweden, Norway, and the Netherlands)[555][556] with his vocal support for far-right parties such as Reform UK[557] and AfD[558] in Germany along with his Nazi salute controversy leading to boycotts of his products and Tesla vehicles being nicknamed Swasticars.[564] German sales fell 76% in February 2025 compared to February 2024.[565][566]

Tesla's shares dropped over 9 percent after its sales in the EU and UK declined by nearly half in January 2025, bringing its valuation below $1 trillion for the first time since November 2024. While European electric car sales surged, Tesla struggled against rising competition, particularly from Chinese automakers.[567] In May 2025, it was reported that the company's sales in Europe declined every month since the start of the year, including in April where sales dropped 49 percent to 7,261 from 14,228 in April 2024.[568] As of May 2025, the company has a 0.7 percent market share in Europe, down from 1.3 percent a year ago.[568]

Board of directors

[edit]

Tesla has received criticism that its board lacks enough independent directors. In an April 2017 public letter, a group of influential Tesla investors, including the California State Teachers' Retirement System, asked Tesla to add two new independent directors to its board "who do not have any ties" with Musk,[585] writing that "five of six current non-executive directors have professional or personal ties to Mr. Musk that could put at risk their ability to exercise independent judgement."[586] Tesla's directors at the time included Brad Buss, who served as chief financial officer at SolarCity; Steve Jurvetson, a venture capitalist who also sits on the board of SpaceX;[587] Elon Musk's brother, Kimbal; and Ira Ehrenpreis and Antonio Gracias, both of whom also invested in SpaceX.[588] The letter called for a more independent board that could put a check on groupthink.[586] At first Musk responded on Twitter, writing that the investors "should buy Ford stock" because "their governance is amazing."[586] Two days later, he promised he would add two independent board members;[589] Kathleen Wilson-Thompson and Larry Ellison were added at the end of 2018.[590] Ellison stepped down in August 2022.[591] Former Tesla CTO J. B. Straubel, who left the company in 2019, was elected to the board in 2023.[592]

Another criticism of the board composition is that most of the independent directors lack automotive industry experience.[593] The exception is Robyn Denholm who served in finance and corporate reporting roles at Toyota Australia from 1989 to 1996.[594]

Other previous board members include businessman Steve Westly; Daimler executive Herbert Kohler;[293] CEO and Chairman of Johnson Publishing Company Linda Johnson Rice;[595] and United Nations Special Envoy on Innovative Finance and Sustainable Investments Hiromichi Mizuno.[596][597]
